label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT — Monday at Embakasi: Friday's pay, what you can say, what you can't, and the Kisumu loading

Brian,

You asked for something you can actually read on Sunday, so this is it. Short sections, and where I can I've given you the words to use rather than just the points. Read the first part before you walk into the yard; the rest is there for when something goes sideways.

DRAFT — Achieng to review before issue. Not circulated yet.


1. THE TWO-MINUTE VERSION

- Friday's pay did not go out. Nobody on the casual list was paid on Friday. That is our failure, not theirs.
- What happened: our bank rejected the payment file on Friday at 1:52pm. A formatting problem in one column — the bank changed its template on 25 November and our file was built on the old one. None of the 212 payments in that file were processed.
- We only saw the rejection after 5pm. The alert went to a finance mailbox we no longer monitor. By then the bank's cut-off had passed and there was no way to pay anyone on Friday.
- The fix: the MD has approved paying the whole list through M-Pesa bulk instead. Money on phones Monday by 11am. That is the earliest, and 11am is the number you hold to.
- Also approved: KES 500 per head for Monday lunch and fare, for every casual on the affected list, paid in the same M-Pesa batch. The M-Pesa charges are on the company — nobody's pay is reduced by them.
- Management apologises in person on Monday. That's you, since I'm travelling. I'll come to how.


2. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED — THE WORDS TO USE

Say it once, plainly, and don't over-explain:

"On Friday the bank rejected our payment file because of a mistake on our side — a formatting error after the bank changed its system. We didn't see the rejection until after the bank had closed for the day, so nothing went out. Nobody's pay was held back, nobody's record is affected, and nobody did anything wrong. It was our mistake and it's on us."

If someone asks why we didn't see it: "It went to the wrong mailbox. That's also on us." Nothing more than that. Don't fill the silence after it — let it sit.


3. WHEN THE MONEY LANDS — AND THE ONE EXCEPTION

- By 11am Monday, on M-Pesa, for everyone whose number is confirmed. 198 of the 212 are confirmed.
- 14 numbers couldn't be reached — mostly the new loaders from the Athi River intake. Peninah will be at Embakasi from 7:30 with a printout. Those 14 need to see her with their ID and the correct number. Their payment goes the same day once the number is verified, but you cannot give them 11am. Say: "same day, once Peninah has your number."
- Peninah is carrying the laptop and will print payslips for anyone who wants one. She's there from 7:30.
- The KES 500 comes in the same batch. Not before it, not separately. Don't let anyone think it's cash on the day.


4. WHAT YOU CAN PROMISE

- Everyone on the list is paid in full, with nothing deducted.
- The money is on phones by 11am Monday.
- The KES 500 lunch and fare is in the same payment, and the M-Pesa charges are on the company.
- Peninah at 7:30 for the 14 numbers and for payslips.
- A management apology, in person, first thing.
- If it is running late, they hear it from you the moment you know — not after.


5. WHAT YOU MUST NOT PROMISE

- Any time earlier than 11am. Not "by 9", not "by lunch", not "any minute now". Mombasa 2024 was a supervisor saying "by lunch" and the money coming at 4pm, and half the shift sitting down. That started with a time we couldn't keep. One time only: 11am.
- Don't tie the money to the trucks. The payment is approved. It lands by 11 whether they load or not. Say that out loud — it takes the only real lever off the table in a way that doesn't cost us anything.
- Don't promise it will never happen again. Say what we've changed — new template, the file checked before cut-off, alerts going to the right mailbox — and leave it there.
- Not a word about contracts, renewals, or "we'll remember this on Monday". Nothing.
- Nothing about the company's finances. If someone asks whether the company has money, the answer is: "I'm not going to discuss company finances. Your pay is approved and it lands by 11." Then stop. Don't fill the gap, don't hint, don't reassure with detail you don't have. This one matters.
- Don't promise that nobody will be spoken to about Monday. Just don't threaten anyone. Discipline stays out of Monday entirely.


6. MONDAY MORNING, IN ORDER

- 5:30 arrive. Walk the yard with Joseph and ask what he's been hearing. Don't open with a speech. Text him tonight that you're coming at 5:30 — he asked who was coming, and he's been holding this alone since Friday.
- Before the muster, get Ouma on his own. Section 8.
- 6:00 muster. Short: apology, the facts, 11am, the 500, Peninah at 7:30. Five minutes, not fifteen. Take two or three questions, not twenty — "anything I can't answer, I'll come back to you before 9."
- 7:30 Peninah at the gate. Announce it at the muster so the 14 actually go to her.
- Loading for Kisumu starts as normal. Trucks out by 9.
- 11:00 the money lands. Confirm to me when you see the confirmations, not before.
- Afterwards, write down what was said, by whom, and the times. Factual, no commentary.


7. THE APOLOGY — HOW TO DO IT

Not defensive. No "the bank let us down", no blaming finance, no "these things happen". Own it, then facts, then stop:

"I want to start with Friday. Your pay should have been in on Friday and it wasn't. That's our mistake, not yours. Nobody did anything wrong. Here's what happened, here's when the money lands, and here's what else we're doing."

One sentence on the bank's template is enough. Then the 11am, the 500, Peninah. Don't apologise and in the same breath ask them to load faster — separate the two, or the apology sounds like a tactic.


8. OUMA

Talk to him first, privately, before the whole group and before he has an audience. He's loud but he's not a bad man, and he's got four kids and rent due like everyone else. He isn't the problem — he's carrying everyone else's anger.

- Ask, don't tell: "What are you hearing? What do the men need?"
- Then give him the same three things as everyone: 11am, the 500, Peninah at 7:30.
- Ask him to help you get the trucks out by 9 — ask him as the man who runs that crew, not as someone being managed.
- Don't argue about last time. Say: "I know we've said tomorrow before. I'm not doing that again. 11 is a time I can keep."
- No side deals. No extra money, no promises about his contract or his group's. If he asks: "I can't do side deals, and you wouldn't want one. Everyone gets the same."


9. IF OUMA'S GROUP WON'T LOAD THE KISUMU TRUCKS

The trucks have to be out by 9 or we lose the mill's offloading slot. But this is a work stoppage, and a stoppage is handled by Operations and HR together — that's you and me, not you alone and not the supervisors on their own. So:

1. Don't confront the group. Ask who's speaking for them. If it's Ouma, you've already spoken to him.
2. Say the truth plainly: the payment is approved and scheduled. It lands by 11 either way. Stopping the trucks won't bring it sooner and won't change the amount.
3. Ask for volunteers. Keep the bays working with whoever will work — Joseph reallocating, supervisors on the ramp, you on the ramp if that's what it takes.
4. Don't send anyone home, don't deduct anything, don't mention contracts or their next engagement. The procedure is explicit: no dismissal and no threat of dismissal on the day. That isn't just policy — it's what stops this becoming a fight.
5. Record names and times, factually. Nothing editorial.
6. If by 8:00 it looks like 9 will slip, call the mill's dispatch desk then, not at 8:55, and tell me.
7. If people who want to work are being blocked or pressured, don't make it a confrontation. Move the loading to another bay if you can, keep people safe, and call me. That's the one thing that changes the picture.
8. Grievances go to Joseph first, then to HR within 48 hours. That's the channel. Stoppages are not a grievance channel and nobody should be told they are. Anyone who wants to raise something, Joseph writes it down and it comes to me.


10. ME

I'm up from 4:30. WhatsApp me before I board — boarding is about 6:30, so anything that changes, before 6:20. I'm in the air roughly 7:00 to 8:20 and I'll have the phone on as soon as we land. If it's a stoppage and you can't reach me, don't improvise anything on discipline or on sending people home. Hold the line in this note and we decide together when I'm back on the ground.

What I need from you: a one-liner before 6:20, even if it's just "all calm"; the count of the 14 who've seen Peninah by 9; confirmation when the batch is out; and anything Ouma says that I should hear.

Nothing in here about the company's finances goes into Monday, in any form. If it comes up, use the line in section 5 and move on.

I'll speak to you Sunday.
A.
